A minor update to a team checklist

Duplication of effort

Over-communicating minor risks to all stakeholders

Daily progress tracking
Which team member completes a task
Scheduling team meetings

Governance Arrangements.q: A project manager is unclear about whether they can commit organisational resources without sponsor approval. What governance issue does this reflect?

Poor communication within the team
Inadequate project planning
Weak technical expertise
Lack of defined authority levels

Acting as the ultimate business owner

Governance Arrangements.q: In a projectised organisation, a programme introduces stricter governance controls. What is the most likely consequence for decision-making authority at project level?

Authority is removed from the project manager entirely

Authority remains unchanged as governance only affects reporting
Authority becomes more decentralised to team members

That stakeholders are fully engaged
That the team can deliver quickly
That the benefits outweigh the costs over time

Better benefits realisation because decisions are made faster
Reduced need for project reporting
Improved strategic alignment because the sponsor is closer to delivery
Undermined project manager authority and confused operational control

Automatic continuation because the benefits remain strong
Immediate termination because cost tolerances will be breached
Adjusting cost tolerances to absorb the overspend
Delegation of the decision to the delivery team

Avoiding formal reviews to save time and effort
Delegating all continuation decisions to the delivery team
Focusing reviews only on updated cost information
Updating the business case and reassessing viability at each stage

Increase reliance on external consultants

Reduce project autonomy entirely

Cost

Continuation due to sunk costs
Delegation of decision to the project team

To transfer accountability from the sponsor to the reviewer

The sponsor approves a major funding decision

Delivery team
Project sponsor
Supplier lead

Increase the overall project budget allocation quite substantially

Increased autonomy for the project team
Elimination of project manager responsibilities

Stakeholders are over-involved

The project manager failed to deliver outputs
The governance structure was incorrect

Stakeholder meeting schedules
Number of team members

Faster overall delivery of the project outputs

The WBS lacks clear structure and decomposition

Focusing only on final deliverables

Explicit statements of what is included and excluded

Elimination of scheduling risks

Requirements were too detailed for early stages

Simplified management of the project risks
Improved accuracy of the project schedule

Leadership.q: Which TWO Belbin roles are MOST associated with challenge and evaluation rather than harmony or delivery execution?

n.0: Performing would not involve renewed conflict.

o: No defects
Higher confidence
Fewer tests
Faster delivery
Less effort
Quality.w: Audits increase confidence in processes.

n.2: Testing is still required.

Quality.q: A project includes multiple suppliers, each with their own quality standards. What should the project manager do during quality planning?
o: Allow each supplier to use their own standards independently
Ignore supplier standards if internal standards exist
Define a consistent set of standards and ensure alignment
Adopt the lowest supplier standard to ensure feasibility
Focus only on final output quality checks
Quality.w: Consistency across suppliers ensures integration, comparability, and overall quality control.

n.1: Supplier standards still influence delivery quality.

Quality.q: A post-project review finds that outputs met specification but failed to deliver expected outcomes. What is the most likely cause?
o: Lack of stage reporting accuracy
Incomplete quality assurance checks
Poor configuration management of products
Ineffective change control during delivery
Weak benefits ownership and tracking
Quality.w: Failure to realise outcomes typically reflects weak benefits management rather than output quality.

n.1: Quality assurance affects outputs, not outcomes.
n.3: Change control issues do not directly explain benefit failure.
n.2: Configuration management relates to product control.
n.0: Reporting accuracy does not drive outcomes.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: A project to implement a new IT system is delayed due to changes in government data regulations. Which aspect of the project context is primarily influencing this situation?
o: Stakeholder communication approach
Project team capability
Project governance structure
Internal organisational culture
External regulatory environment
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Regulatory changes are part of the external environment impacting the project.

n.3: Culture is internal, not the main driver here.
n.1: Capability is not the cause of delay.
n.0: Communication is not the primary issue.
n.2: Governance is not driving the change.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: Which TWO factors are part of the external project environment?
o: Team capability
Internal governance structures
Market conditions
Organisational culture
Regulatory requirements
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Regulations and market conditions are external influences.

n.1: Governance is internal.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: A project is delayed because suppliers cannot meet demand due to global shortages. Which context factor is dominant?
o: Stakeholder expectations
Internal governance
Organisational hierarchy
Project scheduling approach
External economic environment
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Global shortages are external economic factors.

n.1: Governance is not the cause.
n.2: Hierarchy is internal.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: A project sponsor approves the business case but then becomes uninvolved, leaving the project manager to make all major decisions alone. Which governance weakness is most clearly shown?
o: The project manager has delegated too much control
The project team has misunderstood the project objectives
The project lacks a clear delivery methodology
The governance structure is too detailed for the project
Oversight and decision-making authority are not being maintained
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Governance requires active oversight and clear decision-making authority, not just initial approval.

n.2: Methodology is not the main issue; the weakness is governance oversight.
n.0: The issue is not over-delegation by the project manager but lack of sponsor involvement.
n.3: There is no evidence the governance structure is too detailed.
n.1: The problem is decision control, not misunderstanding objectives.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: A project is delivering outputs successfully but is later cancelled because it no longer supports organisational priorities. What does this highlight?
o: Need for continuous strategic alignment
Ineffective resource planning
Failure of project governance
Impact of external environment
Importance of stakeholder communication
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Projects must remain aligned with evolving strategy.

n.4: Communication is not the core issue.
n.2: Governance may be involved but not primary.
n.1: Resources are not the issue.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: A project meets all agreed constraints but is terminated early due to lack of expected benefits. What is the most accurate conclusion?
o: The project should have continued to recover costs
The project should not have defined benefits initially
The project was successful because constraints were met
The project failed because benefits were not realised
The project manager did not control scope effectively
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Benefits realisation is central to success.

n.2: Constraints alone do not define success.
n.1: Benefits must always be defined.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: Which situation most clearly represents a project rather than BAU?
o: Implementing a new enterprise resource planning system
Updating employee records in HR systems
Continuous system maintenance and patching
Processing daily customer orders
Monthly financial reporting using standard templates
Project Management Fundamentals.w: ERP implementation is unique and temporary, aligning with project definition.

n.2: Maintenance is BAU.
n.1: Record updates are BAU.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: A project team selects a delivery approach without considering organisational culture, leading to resistance. What principle has been overlooked?
o: Stakeholder engagement
Risk escalation
Resource optimisation
Strategic alignment
Contextual adaptation
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Projects must adapt to organisational context, including culture.

n.0: Engagement is affected but not the core issue.
n.3: Strategy is not the issue here.
n.2: Resources are not the focus.
n.1: Risk escalation is unrelated.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: A project is technically feasible but conflicts with organisational values, leading to rejection. What aspect of context is most relevant?
o: Stakeholder mapping
Procurement strategy
External market forces
Project lifecycle selection
Organisational culture
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Organisational values are part of internal context.

n.2: Market forces are external.
n.0: Mapping is not the core problem.
n.1: Procurement is irrelevant here.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: A digital transformation initiative is described as ‘ongoing, evolving, and continuously improving processes’. Why is this description problematic when defining it as a project?
o: It ignores the need for ongoing stakeholder engagement
It suggests a complete absence of governance arrangements
It provides no clarity on the defined project outputs
It conflicts with the temporary nature required for projects
It overstates the importance of long-term outcomes
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Projects are temporary; ongoing evolution suggests BAU or programme activity.

n.2: Outputs are not the main issue.
n.1: Governance is not implied.
n.0: Stakeholders are not the defining issue.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: Which TWO elements distinguish outcomes-based success criteria from output-based criteria?
o: Tracking of resource utilisation
Focus on deliverables produced
Measurement of benefits achieved
Assessment of schedule adherence
Focus on value realised after delivery
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Outcomes-based criteria focus on value and benefits.

n.1: This relates to outputs.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: A project manager adapts delivery methods to align with organisational decision-making speed. What is being demonstrated?
o: Resource optimisation
Context awareness
Risk mitigation
Strategic alignment
Scope control
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Adapting to organisational characteristics reflects context awareness.

n.2: Risk is not the main focus.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: A project has strong technical delivery but weak governance. Which risk is most likely?
o: Decisions may be made without sufficient authority or strategic control
Stakeholders will have too much operational involvement
The team will be unable to produce technical outputs
The delivery lifecycle will become linear rather than iterative
The project will automatically exceed its budget
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Weak governance risks poor decision-making, unclear authority and loss of strategic control.

n.2: Technical delivery may still succeed despite governance weakness.
n.4: Budget overrun is possible but not automatic.
n.1: Stakeholder involvement is not the primary stated risk.
n.3: Governance weakness does not determine lifecycle type.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: Which TWO outcomes are most likely when governance structures are unclear?
o: Confusion over who can approve changes
Faster decision-making with no loss of control
Improved accountability across all stakeholders
Delayed escalation of significant issues
Reduced need for reporting
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Unclear governance creates confusion over authority and can delay escalation.

n.1: Unclear governance may appear faster but usually weakens control.
n.2: Accountability is usually weakened, not improved.
n.4: Reporting remains necessary and may become more important.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: Which TWO factors would most strongly indicate that work is NOT a project?
o: The work has no defined end point
The work is governed by budgets
The work is highly repetitive
The work produces deliverables
The work involves stakeholders
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Lack of end point and repetition contradict project definition.

n.4: Stakeholders are not exclusive to projects.
n.1: Budgets apply to both.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: A project board is reviewing a high-risk project. The project manager wants rapid approvals to avoid delay, but the board insists on formal stage-gate reviews. What is the strongest governance justification for the board's position?
o: Stage-gates guarantee delivery within tolerance
Stage-gates remove the need for project manager judgement
The project board should approve all operational decisions
Formal reviews prevent stakeholders changing requirements
Formal reviews provide oversight and control before further commitment
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Stage-gate reviews support governance by controlling commitment and ensuring informed decisions.

n.1: Governance supports judgement; it does not remove it.
n.2: Project boards should not make all operational decisions.
n.0: Stage-gates improve control but do not guarantee delivery.
n.3: Governance does not prevent all change.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: A project is aligned with corporate strategy but fails due to lack of support from senior management. What aspect of project context was underestimated?
o: Internal organisational influence
Technical complexity
External economic factors
Project scheduling constraints
Supplier capability
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Internal influence, particularly leadership support, is critical.

n.2: External factors are not the issue.
n.1: Technical complexity is not mentioned.
n.3: Scheduling is not the root cause.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: A project continues despite no longer supporting business objectives. What does this indicate about its success criteria?
o: They were not communicated to the project team
They were not aligned with organisational strategy
They are overly focused on stakeholder satisfaction
They were based only on quality measures
They were too detailed to be useful
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Success criteria must align with evolving organisational strategy.

n.2: Stakeholder focus is not the issue.
n.4: Detail is not the main problem.
n.3: Quality focus is not the issue.
n.0: Communication is not the primary issue.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: A project governance group receives detailed reports but rarely challenges progress claims or risks. Which statement best describes the weakness?
o: Governance should focus only on financial performance
The reporting cycle should be replaced by informal updates
The project manager is providing too much information
Governance is present in form but ineffective in oversight
The project team should make fewer decisions independently
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Governance must actively oversee, challenge and control, not merely receive reports.

n.2: The problem is not necessarily report volume but lack of scrutiny.
n.4: The issue is board behaviour, not necessarily team independence.
n.1: Informal updates would weaken control further.
n.0: Governance should cover more than finance.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: A project team is tasked with implementing a process used successfully in another division with minimal changes. Which factor most challenges whether this work should be considered a project?
o: The existence of predefined deliverables
The need for formal governance approval
The requirement to deliver within a set timeframe
The presence of stakeholders across divisions
The lack of uniqueness in the work being performed
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Projects require uniqueness; replicating standard processes reduces this characteristic.

n.0: Deliverables exist in both projects and BAU.
n.3: Stakeholders are present in both contexts.
n.1: Governance exists beyond projects.
n.2: Time constraints alone do not define a project.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: During project initiation, a sponsor emphasises that success will be measured by improved customer satisfaction rather than system deployment. What is this primarily highlighting?
o: Outputs should be deprioritised in favour of deliverables
Customer satisfaction is an operational metric only
Outputs and outcomes are interchangeable in project success
Outcomes are more significant than outputs in defining value
Projects should not focus on technical deliverables
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Outcomes represent benefits and value, whereas outputs are deliverables.

n.1: Customer satisfaction can be a project outcome.
n.2: They are distinct concepts.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: A project manager is asked to define success criteria at initiation. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: Focus on outputs rather than outcomes to simplify measurement
Define success only in terms of time, cost, and quality
Include benefits, stakeholder satisfaction, and alignment with objectives
Avoid defining success criteria until delivery is complete
Use only financial measures to ensure objectivity
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Comprehensive success criteria include benefits, satisfaction, and alignment.

n.1: Triple constraint is insufficient alone.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: Which situation most clearly shows misalignment between a project and organisational strategy?
o: A project delivering outputs that do not contribute to strategic objectives
A project delivering its outputs late because of technical setbacks
A project facing sustained stakeholder resistance during its delivery phase
A project encountering unexpected regulatory delays before final approval
A project exceeding its agreed budget through rising supplier costs
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Strategic alignment requires outputs to support objectives.

n.1: Timing is not alignment.
n.2: Resistance is not necessarily misalignment.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: A project is judged successful by senior management but unsuccessful by end users. What does this suggest?
o: Success criteria were not consistently defined across stakeholders
The chosen project life cycle was fundamentally inappropriate
The project delivered outputs of poor technical quality
The governance structures overseeing the project were ineffective
The project significantly exceeded its approved budget
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Different stakeholder perspectives indicate unclear or inconsistent success criteria.

n.2: Quality is not necessarily the issue.
n.3: Governance is not the main issue.
n.1: Lifecycle is not the issue.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: A team delivers a software tool exactly as specified, but users adapt it in unexpected ways to generate additional benefits. What does this illustrate?
o: Outcomes may differ from intended outputs
Outputs should not be defined at project start
Outcomes emerge from how outputs are used
Outputs can directly control outcomes
Outputs and outcomes are independent and unrelated
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Outcomes depend on how outputs are applied in practice.

n.3: Outputs do not fully control outcomes.
n.0: Outcomes do not differ from outputs; they are distinct.
n.1: Outputs must be defined.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: A senior executive bypasses the agreed governance route and instructs the project team to add features directly. What is the most likely consequence?
o: Stronger strategic alignment because the request came from an executive
Undermined project control and weakened accountability
Reduced need for formal change control due to seniority
Lower project risk because escalation has already occurred
Improved stakeholder responsiveness because decision-making is faster
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Bypassing governance undermines control, accountability and formal decision-making.

n.4: Speed does not justify bypassing control.
n.2: Seniority does not remove the need for change control.
n.0: Executive input does not automatically mean strategic alignment.
n.3: Risk may increase because control has been bypassed.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: Which scenario best illustrates a mismatch between defined success criteria and actual project outcomes?
o: A project consumes more resources than were initially planned
A project requires several additional governance reviews before approval
A project meets its schedule but slightly overspends its budget
A project experiences repeated stakeholder conflict throughout its delivery
A project delivers outputs that do not achieve intended organisational benefits
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Success requires benefits, not just outputs.

n.2: This relates to constraints, not success mismatch.
n.3: Conflict does not necessarily mean failure.
n.1: Governance reviews do not define success.
n.0: Resource use is not the main issue.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: Which TWO features are most central to effective project governance?
o: Avoidance of escalation to maintain speed
Unlimited flexibility for the project manager
Clear decision-making authority
Oversight of project performance and risks
Removal of formal controls once delivery begins
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Effective governance requires clear authority and active oversight of performance and risk.

n.1: The project manager operates within delegated authority, not unlimited flexibility.
n.0: Escalation is part of governance when limits are exceeded.
n.4: Formal controls remain important during delivery.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: A project manager escalates a tolerance breach to the project board rather than resolving it alone. What governance principle is being applied?
o: Decision-making should occur at the appropriate authority level
The project manager should avoid accountability for poor performance
Delegated authority must be ignored when uncertainty arises
Escalation is only required when the business case fails
Operational control should sit entirely with the board
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Governance defines authority levels and requires escalation when delegated limits are exceeded.

n.2: Delegated authority is not ignored; it is respected through escalation limits.
n.4: The board should not control all operational decisions.
n.3: Escalation may be required for any tolerance breach.
n.1: Escalation supports accountability rather than avoiding it.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: Which scenario best illustrates the influence of internal context on a project?
o: Currency fluctuations increasing project costs
Competitor activity influencing market demand
A shift in organisational leadership priorities mid-project
Changes in international trade policies affecting supply chains
New environmental regulations impacting materials
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Leadership priorities are part of internal context.

n.1: External competitive factor.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: A project is delivered on time and within budget, but the intended operational improvements are not realised and stakeholders are dissatisfied. Which judgement best reflects project success?
o: The project is partially successful because outputs were delivered
The project cannot be assessed without reviewing technical quality
The project is successful because it met time and cost constraints
The project is successful because governance objectives were met
The project is unsuccessful because benefits and stakeholder satisfaction were not achieved
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Success is defined by benefits and stakeholder satisfaction, not just time, cost, and quality.

n.2: Time and cost alone do not define success.
n.0: Outputs alone are insufficient to determine success.
n.3: Governance success does not equal project success.
n.1: The failure in benefits and satisfaction is already clear.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: Which statement best describes the purpose of governance in a project environment?
o: To remove uncertainty from delivery through formal reporting
To ensure every stakeholder has equal decision authority
To provide structures for oversight, control and accountable decision-making
To replace project controls with senior management judgement
To ensure the project manager personally approves all decisions
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Governance provides oversight, control, accountability and decision structures.

n.4: Governance distributes authority appropriately; it does not centralise all decisions in the project manager.
n.3: Governance uses controls; it does not replace them.
n.0: Governance manages uncertainty but cannot remove it.
n.1: Stakeholders do not all hold equal decision authority.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: A project delivers a high-quality product, but stakeholders reject it because it does not meet their evolving needs. What does this demonstrate?
o: Success criteria must include stakeholder satisfaction and not just technical quality
Stakeholders should not be allowed to influence success measures
Technical quality is the single most important success criterion here
Projects should prevent any requirement changes once delivery begins
High technical quality inevitably guarantees full stakeholder acceptance
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Stakeholder satisfaction is a key success criterion beyond technical quality.

n.2: Quality alone does not ensure success.
n.1: Stakeholders are central to success.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: A manager describes a project as ‘any work that has a start and end date’. What is the most accurate critique of this statement?
o: It ignores the need to engage and involve stakeholders
It overlooks the governance structures that all projects require
It overemphasises delivering outputs rather than achieving useful outcomes
It incorrectly assumes that all BAU work is continuous
It fails to recognise that temporary work must also be unique
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Temporariness alone is insufficient; projects must also be unique.

n.0: Stakeholders are not the defining factor.
n.1: Governance is not part of the core definition.
n.2: Outputs vs outcomes is not the central issue.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: Which TWO scenarios are most likely to be classified as BAU?
o: Maintaining a customer support helpline
Producing weekly payroll reports
Rolling out a one-time organisational restructure
Delivering a new product launch campaign
Developing a bespoke software solution
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Payroll reporting and support helplines are ongoing operational activities.

n.2: Restructure is a project.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: A sponsor defines project success solely as delivering within budget. What is the most significant risk of this definition?
o: The project life cycle may need to be redefined midway
The project may deliver outputs that fail to realise intended benefits
The governance structure may grow unnecessarily complex over time
The project manager may lose authority over key delivery decisions
The project team may neglect stakeholder engagement to protect the budget
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Focusing only on cost risks ignoring whether the project delivers value or benefits.

n.4: Engagement may suffer, but the core issue is benefits.
n.2: Governance complexity is unrelated.
n.0: Lifecycle choice is not the main issue.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: Which TWO factors should be included when defining project success criteria?
o: Avoidance of governance processes
Achievement of intended benefits
Stakeholder satisfaction
Delivery within time constraints
Minimising team workload
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Benefits and stakeholder satisfaction are key success measures.

n.4: Workload is not a success criterion.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: Which statement best reflects a mature understanding of project success?
o: Success is achieved when outputs are delivered as planned
Success is determined by the project manager’s performance
Success depends on delivering benefits and satisfying stakeholders
Success is achieved when risks are minimised
Success is defined by meeting time, cost, and quality targets
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Success is broader than constraints and focuses on value and satisfaction.

n.1: Success is not based solely on the project manager.
n.3: Risk management alone does not define success.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: A project board approves continuation at each stage despite unresolved risks, because stopping would be politically difficult. Which governance failure is most evident?
o: Decision-making is being influenced by avoidance rather than objective control
Project controls are preventing delivery flexibility
The project manager has too much authority over strategic decisions
The board is applying excessive challenge to the project
The governance structure is too independent from the organisation
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Governance should enable objective decisions, including stopping or redirecting work when justified.

n.2: The issue lies with the board's decision behaviour.
n.4: There is no evidence of too much independence.
n.1: Controls are not preventing flexibility here.
n.3: The board is not challenging enough.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: Which TWO characteristics are essential to defining a project in APM terms?
o: Continuous improvement
Temporary nature
Ongoing operational support
Repetitive execution
Uniqueness of deliverables
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Projects are temporary and unique endeavours.

n.2: Operational support is BAU.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: A programme manager claims a long-running internal reporting initiative is a project because it required initial funding approval and produced a new dashboard. The team now continuously updates reports and adds minor features every month. Which judgement best aligns with the APM definition of a project?
o: It is a project because it involves stakeholders and delivers organisational value
It remains a project because it produces outputs that can be enhanced over time
It is no longer a project because the work has transitioned into ongoing operational activity
It is a project only if the dashboard continues to evolve in response to stakeholder feedback
It remains a project because it originally had a defined start and funding approval
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Once work becomes continuous and repetitive, it shifts from temporary endeavour to BAU, even if it originated as a project.

n.1: Ongoing enhancement does not maintain project status; repetition indicates BAU.
n.3: Evolution alone does not define a project; temporariness is key.
n.4: Historical characteristics do not define current classification.
n.0: Value delivery alone does not distinguish projects from BAU.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: A project delivers a new CRM system, but user adoption remains low and sales performance does not improve. Which statement best reflects the distinction being demonstrated?
o: The project delivered outcomes but lacked defined outputs
The project failed because it did not deliver its output
The project delivered outputs but failed to realise outcomes
The project cannot be assessed without stakeholder feedback
The project succeeded because outputs were delivered within scope
Project Management Fundamentals.w: The CRM system is an output, but improved sales is the intended outcome, which was not achieved.

n.1: The output was delivered; failure relates to outcomes.
n.4: Success requires more than output delivery.
n.3: The distinction is clear without further input.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: A construction company repeatedly builds identical housing units using the same design and process. Which classification best applies?
o: BAU only if there are no external stakeholders
A project because each house produces a distinct output
A project because each house has a defined completion date
A hybrid of project and BAU due to repetition
BAU because the work lacks uniqueness despite being temporary per unit
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Repetitive work with minimal variation is BAU, even if outputs are discrete.

n.2: Temporariness alone is insufficient.
n.1: Outputs alone do not define projects.
n.3: Classification depends on characteristics, not blending.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: A project is within budget and schedule, but no one can confirm who has authority to approve a major scope change. Which governance issue is most likely present?
o: Weak benefits tracking
Poor definition of decision rights
Insufficient project monitoring
Overly restrictive project controls
Inadequate risk identification
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Governance structures must define who has authority to make key decisions.

n.2: The issue is not monitoring performance but unclear authority.
n.0: Benefits tracking is not the immediate governance weakness.
n.4: Risk identification does not address approval authority.
n.3: The issue is unclear control, not excessive control.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: Which TWO responsibilities would normally sit with a project governance body rather than the delivery team?
o: Approving continued investment at key decision points
Resolving every operational issue during delivery
Assigning daily tasks to individual team members
Writing detailed technical work instructions
Providing oversight of alignment with organisational objectives
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Governance bodies approve investment decisions and oversee strategic alignment.

n.2: Daily task assignment belongs to delivery management.
n.3: Technical instructions are not normally a governance responsibility.
n.1: Operational issues should usually be managed by the project team unless escalation is needed.

Project Management Fundamentals.q: Which TWO consequences are most likely if success criteria focus only on time, cost, and quality?
o: Better alignment with strategy
Failure to realise benefits
Improved stakeholder satisfaction
Delivery of outputs without value
Reduced need for stakeholder engagement
Project Management Fundamentals.w: Focusing only on constraints risks missing benefits and value.

n.2: Satisfaction may decrease.
